sample.universe: the universe of 2,278,868 children born between 1981 and 2017 in Denmark
sample.unit_of_observation: child (short-run analyses); person-by-age observation (pooled long-run analyses at ages 25-32 or 16-26)

sample.period: births 1981-2017; outcomes observed to 2018-2019 depending on the register
sample.n_observations: 1,230,180 children in the final short-run analysis sample; 1,616,792 to 6,487,930 person-age observations in the pooled long-run regressions

construction_notes: Respiratory disease exposure index: the number of inpatient admissions with an acute respiratory disease primary diagnosis among children aged 13-71 months, per 100 children, in each municipality and calendar year-month, assigned to each month of a child's first year of life by municipality of residence and then summed over the 12 months; the child's own older sibling is excluded from the rate.
Separate indices are built the same way over the first six and the second six months of life.
71 months (5 years 11 months) is the upper age limit, chosen to capture preschool-aged children; Danish children start primary school at age six.
Wages and total income are winsorized at the first and ninety-ninth percentiles and converted into 2010 US dollars.
Income percentile rank is computed in the overall Danish population (not the analysis sample) within each birth cohort and at each observed age.
Labor force participation is an indicator equal to 1 for the employed and for the unemployed who are searching, 0 for those out of the labor force.
Ninth grade Danish and mathematics test scores are standardized within subject and test year to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
Mental health care visits are expressed per 100 individuals per year.
The 2007 municipal reform reduced the number of municipalities from 275 to 98; the current structure is used throughout with a crosswalk, and the final sample contains 91 municipalities.

Standard errors are clustered on the child's municipality of birth in Table 2 and the figures, and two-way clustered on the individual and the municipality of birth in the pooled person-by-age models of Tables 3-7.

Mean values of the disease exposure index are 2.801 for older and 2.895 for younger siblings; mean first-year acute respiratory hospitalizations are 4.7 per 100 older and 9.3 per 100 younger siblings.

claims.statement: Without family background controls, a one-unit higher local respiratory disease exposure index in the first year of life raises the younger sibling's number of acute respiratory hospitalizations in that year by 0.012 more than the older sibling's.

register_source.value: National Patient Register (NPR), inpatient admissions with an acute respiratory disease primary diagnosis, 1981-2018

definition.value: Interaction of an indicator for being the younger (second-born) sibling with the respiratory disease exposure index, where the index is the sum over the 12 months of the child's first year of life of the number of inpatient admissions with an acute respiratory disease primary diagnosis among children aged 13-71 months, per 100 children, in the child's municipality of birth, excluding any hospitalizations of the child's own older sibling. One unit = one additional acute respiratory hospitalization per 100 children aged 13-71 months. The reported coefficient is beta_3 of model (1), the differential effect for younger relative to older siblings.

timing.value: respiratory disease exposure cumulated over months 0-12 of the child's life

outcome.label: Number of acute respiratory hospitalizations, first year of life

timing.value: measured over months 0-12 of the child's life

units.value: acute respiratory hospitalizations per child over the exposure window, per one additional acute respiratory hospitalization per 100 children aged 13-71 months in the municipality

magnitude.interpretation: The interaction is the differential effect on younger relative to older siblings; the younger-sibling main effect falls by more than 80 percent once it is included.

estimand.target_population: younger (second-born) siblings in Danish firstborn/second-born sibling pairs, relative to their older siblings
estimand.time_horizon: effect on hospitalizations during the first year of life

population.description: Firstborn and second-born singleton sibling pairs born in Denmark 1981-2017, from families with more than one child, with birth spacing of at least 11 months, complete municipality-of-birth information, born in municipalities averaging at least 1,000 children aged 13-71 months, and non-missing parental controls; 1,230,180 children.
population.selection: Starting from the universe of 2,278,868 children born in Denmark 1981-2017: drop one-child families; keep only the firstborn and second-born, and only if both are singletons; require birth spacing of at least 11 months; require complete municipality of birth and a municipality averaging at least 1,000 children aged 13-71 months (7 municipalities dropped); drop children with missing parental controls; keep sibling pairs in which both children remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Birth-order variation in susceptibility to intrahousehold respiratory disease spread combined with within-municipality, over-time variation in local respiratory disease prevalence among children aged 13-71 months (driven by irregular seasonal waves of RSV and influenza); the differential effect on younger versus older siblings within municipality of birth and birth year-month.

key_assumptions.assumption: No unobserved municipality-specific time-varying factors that are (i) correlated with respiratory disease prevalence, (ii) influence children's outcomes, and (iii) differentially impact younger versus older children in a family.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Robustness to municipality-specific linear and quadratic trends and to maternal fixed effects; balance tests that use the control variables X as outcomes (Supplemental Appendix Table C3); placebo indices built from noninfectious digestive diseases and from injuries and poisonings (Supplemental Appendix Tables C5-C6). The authors state the assumption is not directly testable.

the impact on respiratory hospitalizations is monotonically decreasing with birth spacing
among short-birth-spacing pairs, effects are larger when the older child attends a childcare center than when it does not

significantly higher effects of disease exposure among infants breastfed for less than half a month (Figure 10); the linear specification implies 15 months of breastfeeding entirely offsets the impact

anchor_quote.text: All of the estimated short- and long-term effects are stronger for disease exposure during the first six months of life, indicating that these first months are a particularly relevant period for policy targeting.

claims.statement: Infancy respiratory disease exposure has no differential effect on the younger sibling's labor force participation at ages 25-32.

register_source.value: National Patient Register (NPR), inpatient admissions with an acute respiratory disease primary diagnosis, 1981-2018

definition.value: Interaction of an indicator for being the younger (second-born) sibling with the respiratory disease exposure index, where the index is the sum over the 12 months of the child's first year of life of the number of inpatient admissions with an acute respiratory disease primary diagnosis among children aged 13-71 months, per 100 children, in the child's municipality of birth, excluding any hospitalizations of the child's own older sibling. One unit = one additional acute respiratory hospitalization per 100 children aged 13-71 months. The reported coefficient is beta_3 of model (1), the differential effect for younger relative to older siblings.

timing.value: respiratory disease exposure cumulated over months 0-12 of the child's life

register_source.value: Register-Based Labour Force Statistics, 1980-2019

definition.value: Indicator equal to 1 if the individual is in the labor force (employed, or unemployed and searching) and 0 if out of the labor force; pooled over ages 25-32.

timing.value: ages 25-32, pooled person-by-age observations

units.value: probability (0-1 scale) per unit of the disease index

magnitude.interpretation: A tested null: the coefficient is -0.000 with a standard error of 0.001 and an interquartile effect size of -0.000.

estimand.target_population: younger (second-born) siblings in Danish firstborn/second-born sibling pairs, relative to their older siblings

population.description: Sibling pairs from the main analysis sample (firstborn and second-born singleton siblings born in Denmark 1981-2017), observed at ages 25-32 as person-by-age observations; cohorts restricted to those observable at those ages, and both siblings required to be observed.
population.selection: Starting from the universe of 2,278,868 children born in Denmark 1981-2017: drop one-child families; keep only the firstborn and second-born, and only if both are singletons; require birth spacing of at least 11 months; require complete municipality of birth and a municipality averaging at least 1,000 children aged 13-71 months (7 municipalities dropped); drop children with missing parental controls; keep sibling pairs in which both children remain.

identification.source_of_variation: Birth-order variation in susceptibility to intrahousehold respiratory disease spread combined with within-municipality, over-time variation in local respiratory disease prevalence among children aged 13-71 months (driven by irregular seasonal waves of RSV and influenza); the differential effect on younger versus older siblings within municipality of birth and birth year-month.

key_assumptions.assumption: No unobserved municipality-specific time-varying factors that are (i) correlated with respiratory disease prevalence, (ii) influence children's outcomes, and (iii) differentially impact younger versus older children in a family.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Robustness to municipality-specific linear and quadratic trends and to maternal fixed effects; balance tests that use the control variables X as outcomes (Supplemental Appendix Table C3); placebo indices built from noninfectious digestive diseases and from injuries and poisonings (Supplemental Appendix Tables C5-C6). The authors state the assumption is not directly testable.

key_assumptions.supported_by: Supplemental Appendix Table C3, following Pei, Pischke, and Schwandt (2019); the authors concede mothers of younger siblings are slightly older and slightly more likely to have a college education at higher index values.

population.description: The roughly 7.6 percent of sample children who can be matched to reported breastfeeding duration in the National Child Database, split into four breastfeeding-duration subsamples.
population.period: births matched to the National Child Database, 2009-2016
population.selection: Starting from the universe of 2,278,868 children born in Denmark 1981-2017: drop one-child families; keep only the firstborn and second-born, and only if both are singletons; require birth spacing of at least 11 months; require complete municipality of birth and a municipality averaging at least 1,000 children aged 13-71 months (7 municipalities dropped); drop children with missing parental controls; keep sibling pairs in which both children remain. identification.source_of_variation: Birth-order variation in susceptibility to intrahousehold respiratory disease spread combined with within-municipality, over-time variation in local respiratory disease prevalence among children aged 13-71 months (driven by irregular seasonal waves of RSV and influenza); the differential effect on younger versus older siblings within municipality of birth and birth year-month.

key_assumptions.assumption: No unobserved municipality-specific time-varying factors that are (i) correlated with respiratory disease prevalence, (ii) influence children's outcomes, and (iii) differentially impact younger versus older children in a family.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Robustness to municipality-specific linear and quadratic trends and to maternal fixed effects; balance tests that use the control variables X as outcomes (Supplemental Appendix Table C3); placebo indices built from noninfectious digestive diseases and from injuries and poisonings (Supplemental Appendix Tables C5-C6). The authors state the assumption is not directly testable.

claims.statement: Infancy respiratory disease exposure has no statistically significant differential effect on the younger sibling's breastfeeding duration (months).

register_source.value: National Patient Register (NPR), inpatient admissions with an acute respiratory disease primary diagnosis, 1981-2018

definition.value: Interaction of an indicator for being the younger (second-born) sibling with the respiratory disease exposure index, where the index is the sum over the 12 months of the child's first year of life of the number of inpatient admissions with an acute respiratory disease primary diagnosis among children aged 13-71 months, per 100 children, in the child's municipality of birth, excluding any hospitalizations of the child's own older sibling. One unit = one additional acute respiratory hospitalization per 100 children aged 13-71 months. The reported coefficient is beta_3 of model (1), the differential effect for younger relative to older siblings.

magnitude.interpretation: A tested null, which the authors read as ruling out changes in breastfeeding as a mechanism driving the long-term effects.

identification.source_of_variation: Birth-order variation in susceptibility to intrahousehold respiratory disease spread combined with within-municipality, over-time variation in local respiratory disease prevalence among children aged 13-71 months (driven by irregular seasonal waves of RSV and influenza); the differential effect on younger versus older siblings within municipality of birth and birth year-month.

key_assumptions.assumption: No unobserved municipality-specific time-varying factors that are (i) correlated with respiratory disease prevalence, (ii) influence children's outcomes, and (iii) differentially impact younger versus older children in a family.

value.normalisation: Older siblings (firstborns, Younger_i = 0) are the reference group; the disease index is scaled as acute respiratory hospitalizations per 100 children aged 13-71 months, cumulated over the relevant exposure window. Not an event study, so no omitted time period.

falsification.condition: The authors state that if the higher first-months hospitalization rates only reflected differential health care system responses rather than real illness, they would not expect to see differences in long-term effects.
